[F9 F10 F11] [NS-1]
C7: The rider's conduct does not evidence a genuine no-show: the rider was contactable and on the way down, the driver's stationary wait of 4 min 0 s (22:42:50–22:46:50) was unannounced traffic-free time outside the app's arrival flow, and the trip was cancelled only 5 min 20 s after the driver first came within 200 m (F2). [F13 F14] [RD-4]
C9: The driver's 90-day record (951 trips, 1 dispute, 0 upheld) is context only and is not used to decide whether the fee stands; it is offered solely for the judge's assessment of account action. [F17 F16] [RD-6]

→ D1 (concedes): Accepted for what it shows and nothing more: the driver was near the pick-up point (F1, F3) — but NS-1 requires all three conditions conjunctively, and 'being nearby' is not one of them; NS-1(i) is the arrival confirmation, which the record says never happened (F6). [F1 F3 F6] [NS-1]
→ D2: The 5 min 20 s inside 200 m (F2) and the platform arrival stamp at 22:41:30 (F5) speak to NS-1(ii)/(iii) only; they cannot supply NS-1(i), which the driver himself concedes is missing (F6, F12) — and the driver's own statement describes a physical wait, not a confirmed arrival. [F2 F5 F6 F12] [NS-1]

[F6 F12 F7] [NS-1 NS-2]

→ D6: There is no profile fact for any 'earned' $4.50 — the facts record only the $6.61 charged to the rider (F7) — and F17's clean 90-day history is context at best; profile facts cannot establish the fee's legal basis and, per the rules, never decide the case. [F7 F17] [NS-1]
→ D7: The clean record actually defeats the driver's implicit justification: no incidents near the route (F14) and fair weather (F15) mean nothing external excused the missed arrival tap, and my brief makes no safety allegation (F9, F10), so no SAFE-1/SAFE-2 escalation arises on either side. [F14 F15 F9 F10] [SAFE-1 SAFE-2]

The admission in F12 that the tap was forgotten does not erase the physical facts it admits the driver was 'there'; F12 is corroborated rather than contradicted by F1 (34 m) and F3 (stationary 40 m from pickup for 4 min 0 s).

events.title: Proposed ruling: refund_full $6.61 (model confidence 0.93)
events.body:
The cancellation was made by the driver, who alleges a rider no-show, so the fee enters through NS-0's "driver cancelled, alleges no-show" branch and stands or falls on NS-1 alone [F4][NS-0]. The trace settles NS-1(i) as failed: no arrival confirmation of any kind is on record — no "I'm Here" tap and no platform automatic arrival (driver_pressed_here_at is null) [F5][F6][NS-1]. Because (i) fails, N-1's conjunctive test cannot be met, and NS-1 is not satisfied no matter how strong the geographic evidence is [F1][F2][F3][NS-1]. NS-2 then applies on its plain terms: where any of (i)(ii)(iii) is unmet, the $6.61 cancellation fee is refunded in full [F7][NS-2]. The amount is fixed by the fare record, not by any computation: the cancellation fee charged is $6.61 [F4][F7], and the trace fixes the amount at $6.61, so refund_full is the outcome.

The platform's logged arrival time of 22:41:30 and the 5 min 20 s inside 200 m are real but cannot supply (i) [F2][F5][NS-1]: NS-1(ii) requires the driver to have been within 200 m at the moment of the arrival confirmation, and the trace marks (ii) and (iii) as failed precisely because there was no such confirmation (0 s measured after a non-existent tap) [F6][NS-1]. The driver concedes the omission in his own statement — "I forgot to press the I'm Here button but I was there" — but a driver's statement is a claim, not the platform confirmation the clause requires [F12][NS-1]. The chat does not cure it either: the driver's own messages at 22:43 and 22:46 place him at the pickup and announce the cancellation, but they are not an arrival confirmation, and the complete timestamped record shows no rider reply [F9][F10][F11][NS-1].

The rider's "I was on my way down" is a statement unsupported by any gps or timeline fact, and the 9 min 50 s from acceptance to cancellation with silence in the chat does show a rider who did not appear [F4][F11][NS-4]. But NS-4 is about rider-initiated cancellation and no rule lets a driver's defective no-show flow stand on substance alone; the rider's remedy for a fee she considers unfair is the NS-7 human appeal, and this ruling recommends the same voucher remedy [F7][NS-7].

NS-2's account action is not triggered: the flag condition is a driver who pressed "I'm Here" while GPS placed him away from the pickup, and no such fake confirmation exists here — the tap never happened [F6][F1][NS-2]. Nor is RD-6 engaged: the breach is a single forgotten tap, and the driver's 90-day record shows 951 trips with zero upheld disputes, so the "repeated" threshold (≥1 prior upheld route dispute) is not met [F16][F17][RD-6]. Profiles are context only and decide nothing [F16][F17][RD-6].

SAFE-1 screen: I read both chat messages, the driver's written statement and the rider's complaint. They contain a pickup identification, a wait-and-cancel notice and an assertion of being on the way down — no threat, intimidation, harassment, sexual remark or dangerous-driving allegation in any direction, so no SAFE-1 or SAFE-2 escalation arises [F9][F10][F12][NS-7]. Evidence is sufficient: the settlement elements (who cancelled, the arrival confirmation, the fee charged, the chat timing) are each on the record, so no gap remains [F4][F6][F7][F11].

claims.assertion: The driver cancelled this RydeX trip and a $6.61 cancellation fee was charged to the rider, so the fee's validity is governed by NS-0's 'driver cancelled, alleges rider no-show' branch.
NS-1(i) fails: the record shows no arrival confirmation at all — the driver never tapped "I'm Here" and the platform recorded no automatic arrival (driver_pressed_here_at is null).

The driver's own written statement admits the missing tap — "I forgot to press the I'm Here button but I was there" — which is a concession on the record, not a substitute for the NS-1(i) requirement.

The closest approach of 34 m at 22:42:45 and the 40 m offset at the stationary position are both within the 200 m data-layer radius, so the driver was geographically close; but proximity alone cannot satisfy NS-1 because NS-1 requires all three of (i)(ii)(iii) and (i) is not met (F6).

Because NS-1(i) is not satisfied, NS-2 applies and the $6.61 cancellation fee must be refunded in full; the $6.61 figure is the fee charged on record (F7), so the amount is computable from the fare fact.

The chat supports the rider: at 22:43 the driver wrote "At the pickup point, silver Toyota Altis" and only at 22:46, three minutes later, wrote "Waited 4 min, cancelling" — the driver treated himself as having arrived while never making the arrival confirmation the policy requires.

The rider's conduct does not evidence a genuine no-show: the rider was contactable and on the way down, the driver's stationary wait of 4 min 0 s (22:42:50–22:46:50) was unannounced traffic-free time outside the app's arrival flow, and the trip was cancelled only 5 min 20 s after the driver first came within 200 m (F2).

No justified-cause defence is available to the driver: no traffic incidents were recorded near the route during the trip window, and the only congestion record is Woodlands Avenue 5 at band 3 (20–29 km/h), which is not the band 1/2 severe-congestion evidence the policy requires.
The driver's 90-day record (951 trips, 1 dispute, 0 upheld) is context only and is not used to decide whether the fee stands; it is offered solely for the judge's assessment of account action.
This brief is limited to the fee and rider status: it contains no threat, harassment or dangerous-driving allegation, so no SAFE-1/SAFE-2 escalation is triggered by the record.

weaknesses: The 'I'm Here' failure is a technical lapse, not proof the driver was absent: F1 (34 m at 22:42:45), F3 (stationary 4 min 0 s only 40 m from pickup) and F5 (arrival recorded at 22:41:30) show the driver really was at the pick-up point, so the judge may find the rider's conduct was in substance a no-show and treat NS-1's tap requirement as a technicality.

The rider's own complaint — "I was on my way down" — is a statement, not a system record, and there is no gps/timeline fact showing the rider was near the pick-up point or in contact with the driver; F11 confirms the chat contains only the driver's two messages, with nothing from the rider. The other side will argue a 9 min 50 s wait (F4) with no rider reply supports no-show.

The judge could find the driver's unconfirmed arrival equivalent to 'platform recorded arrival' under NS-1(i), in which case (ii) (40 m, within 200 m, F2/F3) and (iii) (4 min 0 s > 3 min, F3) would both be satisfied and the $6.61 would stand — my case rests on the literal text of NS-1(i) and F6.

claims.assertion: The driver was physically at the pickup point: GPS puts his closest approach at 34 m (F1), he was stationary at 40 m from the pickup for the full 4 minutes 22:42:50–22:46:50 (F3), immediately before he cancelled at 22:46:50 (F4).

The driver waited at the pickup point for more than 3 minutes after being inside the pickup radius: he first came within 200 m at 22:41:30 and accumulated 5 min 20 s within 200 m before cancellation (F2), and the platform's own timeline records arrival at 22:41:30 with cancellation 5 min 20 s later (F5) — the subscriber waited, and the rider did not appear.

The rider was told in-app, before the cancellation, that the driver was at the pickup point ('At the pickup point, silver Toyota Altis', chat #1 at 22:43, F9), then that he had waited 4 minutes and was cancelling (chat #2 at 22:46, F10); the rider never replied in the complete, fully timestamped chat record (F11), so nothing in the record contradicts the driver's account.

There is no platform arrival confirmation on record — the driver never tapped 'I'm Here' and no automatic arrival was recorded (F6); the driver admits the missed tap in his statement (F12), and his account is undisputed for content by any system record.
The $6.61 cancellation fee on record (F4, F7) is the fee the rider now disputes; surge was 1.0× so no surcharge is in issue (F8) — the only question is whether the no-show conditions were met.

The driver has 951 trips in 90 days at 4.87 rating with zero disputes upheld (F17), and the rider has zero upheld disputes in 90 days (F16); neither profile supports stripping the driver of the $4.50 he would earn from a valid no-show.

Otherwise the record is clean — fair weather, 0.0 mm rain (F15), and no traffic incidents near the route during the trip window (F14) — so there is no competing explanation (e.g. driver diverted away) for the wait, and no safety allegation appears in the complaint or chat (F9, F10).

weaknesses: The fatal gap is the arrival tap: F6 records no 'I'm Here' press and no platform automatic arrival (driver_pressed_here_at is null). Under NS-1 condition (i) the fee requires the driver to have pressed 'I'm Here' (or an automatic arrival), and the driver admits in F12 that he forgot. The rider will argue NS-2 applies literally: where (i) is not met, the $6.61 must be refunded in full, and if the judge reads NS-1 strictly there is no room for a GPS substitute — even though F2 and F5 show he was within 200 m for 5 min 20 s and F3 shows him stationary 40 m away for 4 minutes.

The rider will lean on the complaint itself ('I was on my way down', complaint text) plus NS-2's wording that any missing condition (i)/(ii)/(iii) makes the fee refundable; the system-record defence (F1, F2, F3, F5) answers the substance but cannot manufacture an arrival tap that the record says never happened.

NS-4/NS-8 cuts the other way on fairness: no rule gives the rider a free cancellation for a late or absent driver, but the rider can still use NS-7's human appeal within 30 days, where the tap defect will be re-litigated and a discretionary voucher may be issued.

Under NS-2 a finding that the arrival tap was missing can also be read as button abuse (flag_account); the driver's own statement F12 concedes the omission, so this collateral risk cannot be talked away, only argued down as an inadvertent omission on a single trip, not a pattern (F17 shows no upheld disputes).

points.response: Accepted for what it shows and nothing more: the driver was near the pick-up point (F1, F3) — but NS-1 requires all three conditions conjunctively, and 'being nearby' is not one of them; NS-1(i) is the arrival confirmation, which the record says never happened (F6).

The 5 min 20 s inside 200 m (F2) and the platform arrival stamp at 22:41:30 (F5) speak to NS-1(ii)/(iii) only; they cannot supply NS-1(i), which the driver himself concedes is missing (F6, F12) — and the driver's own statement describes a physical wait, not a confirmed arrival.

The complete timestamped chat (F11) shows the last rider-side silence, but silence is not a no-show finding, and the driver's label 'Waited 4 min, cancelling' (F10) is his own characterisation at 22:46, arriving four minutes after he placed himself at the pickup (F9) — it does not cure the missing arrival confirmation (F6).

This is the decisive point and the driver states it against his own case: NS-1(i) is unmet because the record shows no 'I'm Here' tap and no platform automatic arrival (F6), and the driver admits he forgot (F12); NS-2 then applies on its plain words — any missing condition refunds the $6.61 in full.

Correct on the arithmetic — $6.61, surge 1.0× (F7, F8) — but the fee's validity is exactly what is in issue, and NS-0 routes a driver-cancellation fee through NS-1; with (i) unmet the fee does not stand and NS-2 mandates refund_full.

There is no profile fact for any 'earned' $4.50 — the facts record only the $6.61 charged to the rider (F7) — and F17's clean 90-day history is context at best; profile facts cannot establish the fee's legal basis and, per the rules, never decide the case.

The clean record actually defeats the driver's implicit justification: no incidents near the route (F14) and fair weather (F15) mean nothing external excused the missed arrival tap, and my brief makes no safety allegation (F9, F10), so no SAFE-1/SAFE-2 escalation arises on either side.
Conceded as a framing point: the fee's validity turns on NS-1 as routed by NS-0, and the $6.61 on record (F4, F7) is the sum in issue.

True but incomplete: F6 records no tap and no automatic arrival, yet F5 records that the platform itself logged the driver's arrival at 22:41:30 and that he cancelled 5 min 20 s later — the record contains an arrival time even without a driver tap.

The admission in F12 that the tap was forgotten does not erase the physical facts it admits the driver was 'there'; F12 is corroborated rather than contradicted by F1 (34 m) and F3 (stationary 40 m from pickup for 4 min 0 s).

Accepted that proximity alone is not the test; but NS-1(ii)'s location requirement is satisfied on the system records (F2: first within 200 m at 22:41:30; F3: stationary 40 m away), so only the tap formality in NS-1(i) is in dispute.

This is the whole case in one line: NS-2 only bites if (i) fails, and F5 shows a platform-recorded arrival at 22:41:30, which is the record's own substitute for a driver tap; where the platform records arrival, (i) is met and the fee stands.

The chat they cite helps the driver: F9 at 22:43 places the driver at the pickup point with the car identified, F10 at 22:46 gives a wait-and-cancel notice, and F11 confirms the record is complete and fully timestamped — so nothing in it supports the rider's claim of being 'on my way down'.

The 4 min 0 s stationary period (F3) is exactly the waiting period NS-1(iii) contemplates, and the rider's assertion of being 'on the way down' is a statement with no GPS, timeline or chat fact behind it, since F11 shows the rider sent nothing.
The driver does not claim any RD-4 justified-reroute defence — this is a no-show case, the trip was cancelled before it ran, and F13/F14 are irrelevant to the fee.
The driver's profile (F17: 951 trips, 4.87, zero upheld disputes) and the rider's (F16: zero upheld) are offered only as context against a flag_account and cannot decide the fee either way.
Conceded: the record contains no threat, harassment or dangerous-driving allegation, so no SAFE-1/SAFE-2 escalation arises.
